** Major** · **Functional Correctness** · **Heavy lift** **Bound the GitHub issue address by its encoded length, not by character count.** `GITHUB_BODY_MAX` limits the body in characters, but the body travels percent-encoded in the query string. Each space or newline becomes three characters. Each non-ASCII character becomes up to nine. A 6,000-character body therefore gives an address of roughly 7,000 characters for English text and far more for other scripts. `handle()` sends this address in a `Location` header through `wp_safe_redirect()`. Large response headers can exceed common server buffers. For example, the default `fastcgi_buffer_size` on nginx with PHP-FPM is 4k or 8k. GitHub also refuses very long new-issue addresses. `send()` calls `mark_sent()` at Line 644 before the redirect. If the redirect or GitHub fails, the draft is already `sent`. The form then disables editing and offers no resend. Measure the encoded size when you truncate. Lower the limit to leave room for the title, footer and base address. If you need more headroom, render an "Open on GitHub" link instead of redirecting.

**Release the response before the IMAP save runs at `shutdown`.** `flush()` runs on `shutdown` at `PHP_INT_MAX`. It then opens an IMAP connection and appends the copies. The open and read timeouts are each set to 15 seconds. Under PHP-FPM, the response is sent only after the script ends, including its shutdown callbacks. If the mailbox is slow or unreachable, the request that sent the email can wait for these timeouts. The email has already been sent at that point, so the wait adds no value. Call `fastcgi_finish_request()` at the start of `flush()`, when it exists. The response then completes before the IMAP work starts. Without PHP-FPM, the guard skips the call and the behaviour does not change. Shutdown callbacks with a lower priority number run before `flush()`. Those callbacks still delay the response. This change only moves the IMAP save after the response.

**Cap retry attempts for a copy that the server keeps refusing.** `save()` stops at the first failed `append()` and keeps that copy at the head of the unsaved list. `record()` queues it again. `retry()` then starts with the same copy every five minutes and has no attempt limit. Copies queued behind it are never attempted. A copy that the server always refuses, for example one above a server size limit, therefore blocks every copy already waiting. Failed copies then build up until the queue holds `QUEUE_MAX` items. After that, further failed copies are counted in `dropped`. Copies from a new request are still saved directly by `flush()`, so only the queued copies are affected. A transient outage affects every copy alike. Any cap must therefore be high enough to cover a realistic outage. Store an attempt count on each queued copy. Increase it after each failed `save()`. After a fixed number of attempts, drop the copy and count it in `dropped`. Keep the oldest-first order.

body: Fixed in 831a1a44, in shorter words: a picture with more files than the cap goes alone, its checks sent in groups of that size.

Not changed: heads() treats a transport error at the deadline exactly as put_files() already does on main. The cost of a real connection failure inside that last quarter second is one retry on the next turn, where a repeat failure outside the window is recorded and paused as usual; telling the two apart would need cURL to report which transfers it stopped, which the bundled Requests library does not expose.

Kept as it is, on purpose. The first slide is the one that shows first, so it is the page's first paint (LCP). When it has no smaller copies, `start()` returns false and `kadence_preload()` prints the head's `<link rel="preload">` for it, discoverable before any script runs. Taking the script path instead, only to size later slides, would replace that early preload with one added after the row, for a picture that does not change, in exchange for smaller files on slides that load after the first paint. The changelog states the rule ("the first slide's required"); the README describes what happens when sizing applies.

Unreadable slides: a later slide with no readable metadata keeps its own picture (it is left out of the list and Kadence's CSS shows it, as the head style hides only `.kb-bg-slide` backgrounds until the class goes at DOMContentLoaded at the latest). Nothing is invented for it.

Fixed in bf741882. The picture lookup is now `SEOProStack_Hero_Picture` (`includes/class-seoprostack-hero-picture.php`), and `meta()` also requires `in_folder()`: the address's folder must end with the year and month folder of the attachment's `_wp_attached_file` (only the end is compared, as a CDN or cloud storage can serve the folder under another start). Otherwise `get()` returns null and the row keeps its own picture and the head's preload.

Checked on the test site with the hero attachment: its own address 5 files, its 1536 copy's address 4, a CDN host with the same folder 5, the same file name in `2020/01` or `2025/11` null, an address with no path null.

Not changed: Kadence Blocks has no background size per slide. In Kadence Blocks 3.8.1.1, `class-kadence-blocks-row-layout-block.php` sets each slide's inline `background-size` from the row's one `bgImgSize` (lines 1514-1515, in the slide loop that writes `kb-bg-slide kb-bg-slide-N` at line 1532), so every slide has the size the script reads from the first. A size other than cover or contain on the row already makes `start()` return false.

Fixed in bf741882. The larger-copy check is now `grow()`, run by the ResizeObserver and by a `matchMedia('(resolution: Ndppx)')` change listener for the current `devicePixelRatio`, re-armed for the new ratio each time (`{ once: true }`); browsers without `MediaQueryList.addEventListener` keep the ResizeObserver only. Never a smaller copy, as before.

Checked in Chromium: 1350×940 at DPR 1 showed the 1536 copy; after the DPR went to 2 (DevTools emulation, which does not send the change event itself, so the test called the recorded listener) it showed the full picture and the listener waited on `(resolution: 2dppx)`.

Fixed for no JavaScript in bf741882: `head()` now also prints the old preload of the row's own picture (its AVIF or WebP copy and type, when pages name copies) inside `<noscript>`. Browsers without JavaScript parse it and preload as before; browsers with JavaScript ignore it, so they do not fetch the full picture alongside the chosen copy, which is the point of the change. Checked: PageSpeed's phone with JavaScript off now lists the `fetchpriority="high"` preload on both sized test pages, and with it on, one file of the picture is fetched.

An unconditional preload in the head cannot be added: it would make every browser fetch the full picture too. A content security policy that blocks inline scripts also blocks WordPress's own inline scripts, so it is not a set-up this targets; there the class is never added, so the row shows its own picture from Kadence's CSS.

+<?php
+/**
+ * WordPress's scheduled tasks list (the cron option), for Fixes for other
+ * plugins (SEOProStack_Plugin_Fixes).
+ *
+ * WordPress keeps every scheduled task of a site in one autoloaded option,
+ * cron. Each request reads it once, and every change it makes
+ * (wp_schedule_event(), wp_unschedule_event(), a cron run moving a task to
+ * its next time) writes the whole list back from that copy. A request that
+ * runs long, as a cron run does (90 seconds on one site, writing the list
+ * about 30 times), writes the list it read at the start back over every
+ * change made meanwhile: removed tasks come back, other plugins' changes are
+ * lost, and the next removal of a task that came back fails with "The cron
+ * event list could not be saved" (could_not_set). WordPress refuses a second
+ * copy of a single event, but not of a recurring one, so the copies stay.
+ *
+ * write() applies what the request changed (the tasks it added, changed or
+ * removed since it read the list) to the list as stored now, so changes made
+ * by other requests meanwhile are kept. dedupe() runs once at the start of
+ * each cron run and removes extra copies of recurring tasks: the same task
+ * (hook and arguments) on the same schedule at more than one time.
+ *
+ * SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-3.0-or-later
+ * SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Marcus Quinn
+ * Additional terms (GPL-3.0 section 7(b)): SEOPROSTACK-ATTRIBUTION.txt
+ * Provenance: wpas-5149fc42f5cbc37c. Copies, even of part, keep these lines.
+ *
+ * @package SEOProStack
+ * @since 1.3.152
+ */
+
+if (!defined('ABSPATH')) {
+    exit;
+}
+
+class SEOProStack_Cron_List {
+
+    /**
+     * Register the hooks. write() runs on every write of the list; dedupe()
+     * only in WordPress cron runs (wp-cron.php), before they read which tasks
+     * are due.
+     */
+    public static function init() {
+        add_filter('pre_update_option_cron', array(__CLASS__, 'write'), PHP_INT_MAX, 2);
+        if (wp_doing_cron()) {
+            add_action('wp_loaded', array(__CLASS__, 'dedupe'), 0);
body: Fixed in e98b11c0: `init()` registers `dedupe()` in WP-CLI requests too, so `wp cron event run --due-now` removes the extra copies. Checked on a test site: two hourly copies became one in a WP-CLI request.

Valid, and left as it is. This is the remaining case named in the PR body. When another request has already made the same change, nothing changes in the database, and `update_option()` returns false whatever this filter returns. Returning `$old_value` also returns false, through its "unchanged" check. The only way to report success here is to write a row that has not changed, and core does not do that. The task itself is in the state the request asked for. The message is less common now, since the list is no longer rewritten from old copies.

Keeping the latest copy is deliberate. `wp-cron.php` calls `wp_reschedule_event()`, which adds the next time, before `wp_unschedule_event()` removes the copy that ran. A dedupe in another request between those two steps must not remove the new copy. If it did, the task would be gone once the first run removed its own copy. Keeping the earlier, due copy has that risk; keeping the latest risks at most one skipped run, at most one interval late. On the sites that prompted this, the extra copies were already being run several times per interval (the AI Engine runner up to 5 times), so skipping an extra due copy is the intended outcome. The changelog entry explains why.

**Do not re-learn an address after a failed pinned request.** `settle()` forgets the address before shutdown, but the shutdown `learn()` callback remains registered. The same web request can write the unchanged `SERVER_ADDR` back to `seoprostack_origin_ip`. A subsequent cron or WP-CLI request can then revalidate and repin that address, which violates the fallback contract that requires DNS until a later web request learns the address.
Suggested fix

```diff public static function forget() { + remove_action('shutdown', array(__CLASS__, 'learn'), 10); delete_option(self::LEARNED); } ```

@coderabbitai This is intended, and it does not lead to an unchecked pin. A web request's `SERVER_ADDR` is this server's current address, so it is "a later web request" in the contract's sense. `learn()` (`includes/class-seoprostack-litespeed-crawler.php`) writes only `{"seen": <address>}`, without `ip`.

`learned()` treats an entry without `ip` as unchecked. Before anything is pinned to it, `learned()` runs `elsewhere()` and `reaches_server()`, a HEAD request for the home page pinned to the address, accepted only when LiteSpeed itself answers with no `cf-ray` header. In the cases `settle()` forgets for, that check fails and stores `ip => ''`:

- The address no longer reaches this server (a host move).
- The server cannot reach its own public address (hairpin).
- A CDN answers.

Requests then use DNS, and the check runs again only after an hour. If the failure was transient and the check passes, pinning again is the right result. Checked live: after the address was forgotten, the next web request noted it again, and the next WP-CLI run checked it (1.04 s) before pinning it.

+* Fix: Media in cloud storage revisits a picture kept after one retryable removal failure on its own (GitHub issue #1266). local_result() stored a permanent kept:<signature> mark in _seoprostack_storage_local that only upload --retry-failed (or switching Remove local copies after upload off and on) cleared, so one "kept original is in use" error left the picture's local files in place and held SEO Pro Directory's import drain until its one-hour no-progress stop (41 minutes on one picture, 6 November 2026). The mark is now kept:<signature>:<time> (kept_timed_mark()); kept_now() counts it as kept for KEPT_RETRY (10 minutes), and removable(), remove_local_now() and remove_local_many() check the picture again after that. Marks set by a mismatch, a change or a restore (removal_stopped(), prepare_removal(), restore) stay permanent; --retry-failed and switching removal on drop both kinds (forget_kept_marks()).
